articles.title: Recognising a dental injury that needs urgent assessment
articles.summary: Dental injuries can affect teeth, gums and the jaw; this guide helps communicate what happened without attempting treatment.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Recognise what happened
paragraphs: A knocked, cracked or displaced tooth, mouth bleeding, or a jaw injury can require prompt dental or emergency assessment. The appearance alone does not reliably show the extent of damage.
Note whether the injury followed a fall, collision or another event, and whether there are other injuries that may be more urgent.

sections.title: Describe the concern
paragraphs: Record when the incident occurred, which part of the mouth seems affected and any difficulty speaking, swallowing or breathing. Do not delay urgent help to complete a record.
Contact an urgent dental service or appropriate emergency service for advice; the correct route depends on the symptoms and severity.

sections.title: Preserve accurate information
paragraphs: If a professional gives specific instructions, follow those rather than relying on a general offline article. Avoid trying to reposition a tooth or jaw based on an unreviewed diagram.
Share relevant medical information and the circumstances of the incident with the clinician.

articles.title: Suspected button battery swallowing: information for an emergency call
articles.summary: A suspected swallowed button battery is time-critical even when a person appears well.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Recognise the possibility
paragraphs: Small button batteries may be found in toys, remotes and other household items. A missing battery and a possible swallowing event warrant immediate emergency assessment; symptoms may initially be absent.
Do not wait for discomfort or visible injury to decide whether to seek help.

sections.title: Contact emergency care promptly
paragraphs: Seek emergency medical help immediately if a button battery may have been swallowed. Tell the responder what is suspected and approximately when it may have happened.
Do not try to make the person vomit or attempt an improvised retrieval. Follow the emergency service's individual instructions.

sections.title: Share the product details
paragraphs: If it can be done without delay, identify the device or battery packaging and provide the size or type shown on it. Uncertainty should be stated plainly.
Keep any available product information for the clinical team, but never postpone urgent assessment to search for it.

articles.title: Suspected swallowed magnets: recognising a serious hazard
articles.summary: Multiple swallowed magnets, or a magnet with another metal object, can cause serious internal injury.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Understand the risk
paragraphs: Small high-strength magnets can be mistaken for harmless play pieces. More than one swallowed magnet, or a magnet with another metal object, may cause serious internal harm.
Symptoms may not appear immediately, so an apparently comfortable person cannot be assumed safe.

sections.title: Seek professional assessment
paragraphs: If swallowing is suspected, seek urgent medical assessment and explain the number and type of objects that may be missing. Do not wait for pain or other symptoms.
Do not attempt home remedies or induce vomiting. Follow advice from the receiving emergency service.

sections.title: Provide a factual account
paragraphs: Record the time last seen with the object and whether other magnets may be missing. Bring packaging or a matching unused item if it is immediately available and safe to carry.
Do not delay assessment while searching for missing pieces or trying to prove exactly what was swallowed.

articles.title: Recognising possible chemical exposure to the eyes
articles.summary: An eye splash involving cleaning or industrial products needs prompt professional advice.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Identify the exposure
paragraphs: Cleaning agents, solvents and other products can injure eyes. The substance, concentration and time of exposure matter, but the appearance of the eye is not a reliable measure of safety.
Avoid approaching spilled material or exposing another person while gathering information.

sections.title: Escalate without delay
paragraphs: Seek immediate appropriate emergency or specialist advice after suspected harmful eye exposure. Follow the responder's instructions for the specific product and situation.
This draft does not provide a treatment sequence or substitute for first-aid training. Do not delay seeking help to read the whole article.

sections.title: Keep useful details
paragraphs: When safe and readily available, provide the product name and label or safety information to the professional. Describe what happened without guessing the chemical identity.
Do not mix products or perform improvised chemical neutralisation.

articles.title: Recording a tick bite and recognising when to seek medical advice
articles.summary: A short factual record can help a clinician assess a possible tick-related illness.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Understand the context
paragraphs: Ticks may attach to skin after time in grassland, woodland or gardens. Not every bite leads to illness, and a person's symptoms and exposure history matter more than assumptions.
Record the approximate date and location of exposure if known, without sharing a private home address unnecessarily.

sections.title: Notice changes
paragraphs: A spreading rash, fever or other new symptoms after possible tick exposure should be discussed with an appropriate healthcare professional. Not all relevant rashes look the same.
Do not use photographs or this offline article to diagnose an infection or decide that symptoms are harmless.

sections.title: Prepare a concise account
paragraphs: Note when a tick was noticed, what symptoms appeared and whether professional advice was sought. If a tick is still attached, use current reputable first-aid guidance or seek help rather than relying on an unreviewed diagram.
This guide deliberately omits removal technique until clinical review is completed.

articles.title: Possible frostbite: recognising a cold-related injury
articles.summary: Cold exposure can damage skin and deeper tissues, requiring careful assessment.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Recognise the concern
paragraphs: Skin that becomes unusually numb, pale, hard or discoloured after cold exposure may indicate a cold injury. Severe cold exposure can also be associated with hypothermia.
The exact appearance varies; do not use a colour chart alone to decide whether an injury is mild.

sections.title: Prioritise safety and assessment
paragraphs: Move away from ongoing environmental danger when it is safe to do so and seek appropriate medical assessment, particularly for persistent numbness, blistering or extensive injury.
Do not rub or mechanically manipulate affected skin based on unreviewed instructions. Follow professional advice for the situation.

sections.title: Describe the exposure
paragraphs: Record the conditions, approximate duration, affected area and any associated symptoms. Mention other injuries or changes in alertness to responders.
Treatment diagrams, warming methods and clinical grading are deferred for specialist review.

articles.title: Lightning incidents: recognising the need for emergency response
articles.summary: A lightning strike or nearby strike can cause serious injury even when external marks are limited.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Recognise the event
paragraphs: A direct or nearby lightning strike may affect the heart, nervous system, hearing or skin. A person may have serious injuries without obvious external burns.
An ongoing thunderstorm can endanger bystanders as well as the affected person; do not create another casualty.

sections.title: Contact emergency services
paragraphs: Call emergency services promptly for anyone suspected of being struck by lightning. Give the location, what was observed and whether there are continuing hazards.
Follow the dispatcher’s instructions. This draft does not teach resuscitation or other emergency procedures.

sections.title: Prepare a useful handover
paragraphs: Share whether the person collapsed, lost consciousness, experienced breathing difficulties or sustained a fall, without trying to diagnose the injury.
Any instructional rescue or treatment diagram must be approved by qualified experts before inclusion.

articles.title: Recognising a potentially serious crush injury
articles.summary: Heavy-object and compression incidents can cause hidden damage as well as visible injuries.
articles.illustration_review_note: Potential recognition or response illustration requires clinical review; no procedural diagram supplied.

sections.title: Understand the situation
paragraphs: A trapped or compressed body part may be injured beneath the skin, and prolonged compression can have serious systemic effects. The absence of major bleeding does not rule out danger.
Machinery, unstable loads and damaged structures can present continuing hazards to helpers.

sections.title: Seek urgent professional help
paragraphs: Call emergency services for serious entrapment, major compression or concerning symptoms. Describe the object involved, whether the person remains trapped and any danger to responders.
Do not attempt hazardous lifting, machinery operation or improvised release procedures from an unreviewed article.

sections.title: Communicate observations
paragraphs: Note the approximate time and duration of compression if known, visible changes and any changes in alertness or breathing. Avoid making clinical predictions.
Specialist rescue, release and treatment instructions are intentionally excluded pending professional review.
